titleStmt.title: Canto 7: tuyil eḻuppiya kātai
The Canto in which [Maṇimēkalā Teyvam] rouses [Cutamati] from Sleep (134 lines)

summary.p: 7.1-14 (14 lines) Action. Maṇimēkalā Teyvam goes to Utayakumaraṉ, who has just passed a sleepless night of love-sickness after seeing Maṇimēkalai in the grove (Canto 5). She urges him to give up his pursuit, for the sake of good kingship.

7.15–40 (26 lines) Action. Maṇimēkalā Teyvam then appears to Cutamati and explains that she has magically transported Maṇimēkalai to the island of Maṇippalavam while Cutamati was asleep (end of Canto 6). She explains that Maṇimēkalai will learn about her previous births there, before returning to Pukār in disguise, and then revealing herself to Cutamati. She further instructs Cutamati to tell Mātavi about the prophecy that she, Maṇimēkalā Teyvam, had given to Kōvalaṉ at the time of their daughter's naming ceremony.
7.41-63 (23 lines) Extended Description. The nighttime activities of the people of Pukār.

7.64–86 (23 lines) Extended Description. The nighttime sounds of Pukār as overheard by Cutamati as she leaves the pleasure-grove: (1) royal timekeepers telling the hour; (2) the trumpeting of an underfed elephant; (3) tuṭi drummers; (4) the songs of drunken artisans; (5) women bathing ritually after childbirth; (6) warriors making prayers at the crossroads to destroy their enemies; (7) the incantation of mantras by magicians to ward off pēy from women who have just given birth.
7.87–93 (7 lines) Action. Cutamati goes from the Buddha’s Flower Grove to the Cakkaravāḷakkōṭṭam and enters the ulaka vaṟavi (‘World Assembly’).

7.94–110 (17 lines) Direct Speech. An image on a pillar addresses Cutamati, recounting her past birth as Vīrai, Maṇimēkalai's sister; the image, like Maṇimēkalā Teyvam earlier in this canto, predicts Maṇimēkalai's return to Pukār in seven days with knowledge of her previous birth(s).
7.111–126 (16 lines) Description. The arrival of the dawn in Pukār.
7.127–134 (8 lines) Direct Speech. Cutamati reports to Mātavi the events of the previous night. Both lament.

div.p: ēḻāvatu maṇimēkalā teyvam uvavaṉam pukuntu cutamatiyait tuyil eḻuppiyapāṭṭu.
The seventh song, in which Maṇimēkalā Teyvam enters the pleasure-grove and rouses Cutamati from sleep.

lg.l: who had seen Maṇimēkalai in the flower grove,

was in despair Lit. ‘[deep-]felt anguish/ heartache/despair/misery having reached [him]/ having attained [deep-]felt anguish/ heartache/despair/misery’. ADD refs and note on semantic range of tuyar and other words for sadness/sorrow etc. Link to Buddhist themes. Cf. the use of the word tuyar in Cilapp and caṅkam
‘By the end of the night, I'll have her in the palm of my hand.’Lit. ‘she [will be] inside my hand’.

He was sitting up, avoiding going to bedTwo options: a) take iruntōṉ as a separate verb (as in Early Old Tamil): lit. ‘being one who sat [up], not going to [his] bed’; b) take iruntōṉ as a modal auxiliary modifying poruntāt': lit. ‘being one who continually avoided going to his bed’ (typical of Middle Old Tamil and later)
—though his bed was as soft as the foaming [sea]—FORMULA. Cf.
when the Goddess appeared before him and said:
If the sceptrei.e. the Cōḻa King's sceptre. FORMULA. Cf. THEME. wavers in its position, the planets will swerve from their course.
If the planets swerve from their course, there will be excessive drought.
If there is excessive drought, there will be no lasting life.Or: ‘living beings will cease to be’
The king who rules the earth will become unworthy to call all living beings his own.(Lit. ‘to call all living beings his life’.)
that you have adopted towards the girl who has undertaken a path of penance!’
[Maṇimēkalā Teyvam], having entered the pleasure-garden [and] snatched Cutamati, who was taking [deeply-] felt sleep there, from the midst of sleep, said:
‘In order to see [the festival] of the thunder of Indra in this city,
I came. Fear not! I, Maṇimēkalai–
because for the young creeper the hetu (reason) has ripened,
[the reason] that put [her] on the path of dharma [laid down] by the primeval, supreme sage (the Buddha) –
having taken away your [girl with] shining jewels by magic,
have set her down, without a single deceit, on the island of Maṇipallavam.
Having realised all [her] previous birth(s)–in a way that the qualities [of her previous births] will have been felt–
the good, artless creeper will come and appear here,
seven days from today, in this city –
even though she will reach [here] in disguise (lit. having concealed [her true] form), she will not hide [her true] nature [from] you.
On that day when that girl enters this city there,
the hetu that shine/occur here will be many.
To Mātavi, the way in which I came,
and the way in which her daughter took to the faultless path,
tell! She knows my nature/history/ methods/affairs/reasons.
On the good day at midnight (lit. in the middle of darkness) when Kōvalaṉ gave (lit. made) my name to this creeper-waisted [girl], declaring/asserting [to Mātavi]:
"There is one deity in the depths of the big/dark waves,"
I told [Kōvalaṉ or Mātavi or both] in a dream, [which seemed] as though [he were] awake,
that, "You have begotten a creeper of very great austerity
who will cut away fierce faults, so that Kāma will be rendered impotent."
Tell to (i.e. remind, since she already knows) that woman there [Mātavi] these matters here!’ so saying,
there the rare deity [Maṇimēkalā Teyvam] rose up into the aether and left; after she had left –
Cutamati, having reached [a state of] fierce sorrow, [and] having got up there (i.e. in the uvavaṉam);
like/together with the dancing girls of the dancing hall/stage, who bring the dance together
by showing the kamala-vārttaṉai gesture to the people who know/understand/are conoisseurs of [all the different] types [of dance-gestures],
together with [their] [dance and music] teachers in the dancing hall(s) of the wide house(s);
The sweet strings of the yāḻ’s notes which sound the [different] note branches,
having enjoyed - better to take as pass aux. ‘the strings having been combined’ combining musical-sounds with the band (i.e. the other instruments) which is skilled in melodies/keeping time,
while [the female players’] red hands heaped with bangles
wander according to [their] nature, not feeling the hot heat which strikes [their] soft fingers;
[and] while those [women] who go to sleep with/despite jealous-sulking, not noticing as [their husbands] try to pacify [them],
being unable to bear [their] worthless husbands’ consorting with other women,
resembling weak creepers there, [their] collyrium-[lined] eyes having reddened,
embrace [their] husbands who fall [with them]/their beloved husbands [on] beds of fragrant flowers;
while the nannies (lit. watch-women) – having scattered Margosa plant (as protection against evil spirits),
for the toddling sons (lit. of short gait) with pratlling red mouths,
sleeping [in their] beds, [with] aimpaṭaittāli [round their necks],
after not staying with the weak legged group [of nannies] (lit. slack-gait-group), running [away],
pulling [their] little toy chariots, [and] hurting themselves –
having waved the incense [over the children] (lit. shown i.e. to god), stay in sleepy sleep;
the intoxication/hilarity having come to an end; the eyes of the drums having fallen asleep;
at midnight when the ancient city, victorious of old, was taking to [its] bed /taking rest.
The incantatory murmuring sound of the time keepers’ praising [the king]/proclaiming [the hour]
by means of the little water pot at the king‘s palace;
and the frenzied-sound of an elephant’s long cry for help as it suffers fully,
because of the agony of starvation, [an elephant] who has been captured and is standing inside a stall;
and the sound of the Tuṭi-drums beaten by the city watchmen
on both the streets where chariots roam and the narrow lanes;
and the drinking songs experienced because of the intoxication by fruit [alcohol]
of artisans who have assembled on [their] boats at the front ghat by the thundering waters [of the ocean]
having engaged in drinking tōppi toddy, which they have brewed by stirring;
and the confused-sound of bathing in the pond by women whose labour is over,
whose stress of recent delivery is over, [women] who have given birth to sons (or perhaps children?)
[using] incense held up by the women, who mixed
snake-mouth [neem - or could this refer to a plant that protects from snake bites] kaṭippakai [and] white-mustard kaṭippakai;
and the sound of offerings being placed with clamour of thunderous voices
saying, ‘May [our] king with bannered chariots achieve victory!’
at the crossroads [haunted by] bhūta, [voices] of men resembling packs of tigers,
for the sake of the elimination of men (i.e. enemy warriors) with hearts compelled [to fight];
and the long[-drawn out] sound of the voices of people throwing offerings, as they stand/constantly throwing (adv. niṉṟu),
[people who recite] mantras/spells to get rid of the suffering
saying, ‘Let the pēy come to the common and take up [their offerings]!’
[the suffering] of those who have experienced a long[-lasting]/long in length wound: women with a fierce/ first pregnancy,
young women who have given/are giving birth, [and] helpless/disabled babies;
all the many different sounds spread and reverberated together.
[Cutamati], having heard [the above sounds, and] having become perturbed at heart, in the depths of the [all-]suffusing darkness—
[and] having gone [from] the flower grove by the little bowered walk-way through overhanging trees [which led along] the western side of the perfect fortress
which she had been told about by the very great deity [Maṇimēkalā]—[and] having extolled and raised [Cakkaravāḷakkōṭṭam] up,
[she] sat down to one side of the World Assembly,
[which has] a portal with split doors that are opened for many people to enter.
of long standing on a pillar, and which reveals [to humans] the causes [of past events]–
while the girl with broad kajal-[lined] eyes [Cutamati] being one who was confused, was frightened–
began to speak of divine [things] with a divine speech:
‘O great/eldest only/unique daughter of Iravi-vaṉmaṉ [Cutamati’s father in previous birth]!
O wife/queen of [King] Tuccayaṉ [Cutamati’s husband in previous birth] with [his] armies of horses!
When Tārai [Mātavi in previous birth, accord. to P.] with a garland of glittering clusters, met with death,
dazed, you who left [the land of] living beings in front of an elephant!
O daughter of Kaucikaṉ [Cutamati’s father in this birth] from [the town of] Caṇpai, of the Kārāḷar tribe!
Having entered this city with Mārutavēkaṉ,
o Cutamati, who used to be Vīrai together with [your] older sister Tārai, listen!
On the seventh day from today, at midnight in the middle of darkness,
having realised your [previous] birth together with her own [previous] birth,
the young girl [Maṇimēkalai] will come to you here, she who used to be Ilakkumi.
Do not fear!’ Thus was spoken [by the image]. Having heard that speech,
the good girl with fine jewels begins to experience trembling at heart.
While the eyes of the guards took sleep;
while sleeping eyes [of people] on pure soft beds opened;
while the [sound of] the right-spiralling conch rose up and roared hollowly;
while the assembly which acts wisely thundered meaningfully;
while the spotted-faced elephant sounded [its] long cry;
while the spotted-feathered fowl sounded [its] short cry;
while many horses in their stables reared up and danced about/made a racket;
while all the many birds in the bamboo/branches rose up and danced about/made a racket;
while the birds/bees whose food is [in] the flower grove increased [their humming/twittering] sounds;
while the bangles on the arms of the flower-creeper like women increased [their jangling] sounds;
while offerings of flowers on the pedestals of gods came to an end/were completed;
while the colourful offerings on the benches/stalls where precious-goods are announced for sale came to an end;
while [the music of] musicians at every gate/door spreading [with their] musical instruments rises up;
while sellers at every shop spreading [with their] merchandise got up;
the rayed [sun] sprung up, sweeping away the black darkness
over the depths of the strong water (i.e. the sea), so as to rouse the city from sleep.
Thrown into an agony of grief like a peacock with an arrow [in its foot] so that [its] feet are in pain,
[Cutamati], having passed along the streets of the great city,
everything that had happened during the previous night. As soon as she had done so,
like a snake which has lost its good gem, she [Mātavi]
bore the unique misery of her daughter not coming.
Cutamati, who had recounted what had happened
was like a body/like [a someone with a] body which has lost [its] sweet life.
